summary: This experimental document describes how S/MIME can be extended to secure message header fields defined in RFC 5322. This offers integrity, non-repudiation, and confidentiality for headers, not only the message body.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally only the letter inside is sealed, not the envelope. This experiment lets the writing on the envelope be locked too.

questions: how to sign email headers with s/mime
subtitle: Protecting email message headers with cryptographic signatures and encryption.

tldr.problem: Email messages can be encrypted and signed, but by default S/MIME only protects the message body, leaving headers like Subject, From, and To exposed to tampering or interception.
tldr.mechanism: This extension embeds selected message header fields inside the cryptographic signature and applies encryption controlled by special gateway servers, so headers get the same protection as the body.
tldr.outcome: Email systems can now guarantee integrity, authenticity, and confidentiality of headers as well as message content, though adoption requires both client and gateway support.

today: RFC 7508 is an Experimental RFC that defines a mechanism for protecting email headers with S/MIME. It has not been obsoleted and remains available for implementations that need header-level security in email systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The S/MIME standard secures email by encrypting and signing message content. By default, S/MIME protects the message body while leaving header fields like Subject, From, To, and custom headers visible and unprotected. The RFC notes that S/MIME does provide one alternative: wrapping a full MIME message in a message/rfc822 envelope to apply security to headers, but this approach lacks guidance on which headers to protect, how clients should reconcile inner and outer headers, and how to handle failures.

This document defines Secure Headers, an extension that uses the signed attributes of the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) to embed selected headers inside the digital signature, giving them integrity, non-repudiation, and confidentiality protection alongside the message body.
sections.plainLanguage: Email security normally seals the letter but leaves the envelope visible. This adds a way to lock up the envelope too.

sections.title: The Problem with Unprotected Headers
sections.content:
Several existing protocols claim to address header protection but fall short. DKIM signs domain-level headers for integrity but does not provide confidentiality and acts at the domain, not the sender level. STARTTLS and TLS with IMAP provide secure channels between email components (MUA, MSA, MTA) but do not guarantee end-to-end integrity since a message can be intercepted after the channel closes. A draft specification called Protected Headers offers integrity via digest values in signed attributes, but if a protected header is altered, the original value cannot be recovered by the recipient, and encryption cannot keep headers private when they must remain visible during transport.

Secure Headers addresses all these gaps by embedding the full header field names and values inside the signature and allowing a trusted gateway (a Domain Confidentiality Authority, or DCA) to optionally remove or replace headers during encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Other systems protect some things about email, but not in the way this spec does. This method lets you seal headers completely, not just check them.

sections.title: Architecture and Header Statuses
sections.content:
Secure Headers involves two participants: the sender's Message User Agent (MUA) and a Domain Confidentiality Authority (DCA) gateway that may encrypt the signed message.

Each header field in the signature carries a status that controls how encryption treats it. A status of duplicated (the default) means the header is signed but also left visible in the message. Deleted means the header is signed but removed during encryption to keep it confidential. Modified means the header is signed but replaced with a different value (such as a placeholder) during encryption, which preserves confidentiality while informing non-compliant clients that secure headers are in use.

The MUA performs signature generation and verification. The DCA performs optional encryption and decryption. Non-conforming S/MIME clients ignore the secure headers attribute and perform standard verification, so backward compatibility is preserved.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to handle a sealed header: leave it visible, hide it completely, or replace it with a different message. The system that signs the email picks which one for each header.

sections.title: Signature Generation and Verification
sections.content:
When an MUA generates a signature with Secure Headers, it takes each header field to be secured, applies a canonicalization algorithm (either simple or relaxed), and embeds the name and value into a SecureHeaderFields structure inside the CMS signed attributes. The same structure also carries the canonicalization algorithm type. The message digest is then computed over the content and the signed attributes together, per standard CMS.

At the receiving end, the MUA verifies the signature and then compares each header in the SecureHeaderFields structure with the corresponding header in the message, using the same canonicalization algorithm. If the canonicalized values match, the header is valid. If any header is missing, altered, or unexpected, the MUA marks the signature invalid and warns the user. The MUA must also display the name, value, and status of each secure header and the canonicalization method used.

The relaxed canonicalization algorithm is recommended for interoperability, as it allows minor modifications like extra spaces or line reformatting without breaking verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The system scrambles headers with a recipe (called canonicalization) so small changes don't break the lock. When the email arrives, it re-scrambles the headers with the same recipe and checks if they match.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption by Gateway
sections.content:
If encryption is required, the sender's DCA gateway intercepts the signed message and processes each header according to its status. Headers marked duplicated are left as-is. Headers marked deleted are removed from the message (except mandatory headers required by RFC 5322). Headers marked modified have their values replaced by new text configured in the DCA.

At the receiver's end, the DCA gateway performs the inverse operation. When decrypting, it restores deleted headers by reading the values from the signature, and it corrects modified headers to their original values from the signature. This ensures the MUA receives all the header information needed to verify the signature.

The encryption and decryption logic is applied only to signed messages that include a SecureHeaderFields structure, ensuring that non-compliant gateways do not interfere with the headers.
sections.plainLanguage: A trusted gateway can hide headers when the message travels, then restore them at the destination so the receiver can verify everything is correct.
